newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese government threatens early election.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese government threatens early election.

text.p: Portugal's Socialist government threatened on Wednesday to call early elections over opposition plans for local government financing which it said would break the budget and block the country's entry to Europe's single currency.

Planning Minister Joao Cravinho issued the warning after a cabinet meeting at which the government, which is four seats short of an outright parliamentary majority, approved its own draft project to reform local authority funding.
"For me, the taxpayers should be given their say at the ballot about a...programme that is based on an increase in taxes," the minister told journalists, referring to opposition plans.

The government says that the various proposals presented by the main opposition Social Democrats and two smaller parties in parliament would mean either a sharp increase in overall taxes or a widening in the budget deficit.
Keeping a tight rein on the budget is a key condition for entry to the European Union's planned single currency which the Portuguese government is pledged to join from its start in 1999.
Parliament approved on Wednesday night the general text of the opposition proposals which is only the first step towards their eventual adoption by the legislature.
They now pass to a special committee on local government for detailed discussion and a final vote by the chamber. It is at this point that the government threat could be put into effect.
The opposition parties deny their plans would hurt the budget and accuse the government of political scare tactics.
The issue of local government financing has become the focus of fierce political debate as parties begin gearing up their campaigns for local authority elections due in December.
A general election is not due until 1999.

The government's own plan, which should be presented to parliament on July 9, would switch some 16 billion escudos ($900 million) of central government expenditure to the local authorities in 1998 as well as devolving some powers.
It says this can be achieved without endangering budgetary targets which call for a state deficit of below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the limit for entry to the single currency.

Branding the opposition ideas "irresponsable", Cravinho said that they would imply an increase of between 10 and 15 percent in income tax and "make it impossible for Portugal to participate in the founding of the single currency".
